> 摩诃是大。人之心量广大，犹如虚空，无有边畔，亦无方圆大小。

The Sanskrit word is *mahā*. Every translation says "great". The sutra text says great, and then spends a paragraph explaining that greatness here has no size.

No edges. No square, no round. No blue, yellow, red, white. No above or below, no long or short. No anger or delight, no right or wrong, no good or evil.

Read that list of negations and notice what kind of definition it is. It is not a measurement that happens to be very large. It is a definition by removal: whatever property you name, greatness is not that. A magnitude can be compared; this cannot. That is why the chapter can call the mind *mahā* and mean something closer to *unbounded* than to *vast*.

## A practice, not a recitation

The full phrase is 摩诃般若波罗蜜 — great wisdom, gone to the other shore. The text gives the translation and immediately moves the term out of the mouth:

*This must be practiced in the mind; it does not lie in recitation. Reciting with the mouth while the mind does not practice is like an illusion, like a transformation, like dew, like lightning. Reciting with the mouth and practicing with the mind, mouth and mind correspond.*

The image for mouth-only practice is taken from the Diamond Sutra's own closing verse — dew, lightning, a conjured thing. A recitation that does not move the mind is placed in the same category as a magic trick: it appears, it is impressive, it is gone.

## 第一莫著空

Then the warning that anyone who teaches emptiness has to give, and usually gives too late:

*Do not, hearing me speak of emptiness, immediately cling to emptiness. Above all, do not cling to emptiness. If you sit quietly with an empty mind, you are clinging to the emptiness of non-recording.*

*无记空* is the technical term: a blank. Not clarity, not absence of clinging — a state in which nothing is registered because the registering has been suppressed. The book treats this as the common failure of people who have understood the vocabulary and not the direction: emptiness becomes a place, and then they sit in it.

The counter-image is a container. Space holds sun, moon, stars, mountains, rivers, springs, good and evil people, heavens and hells, all the oceans, Sumeru — *all within emptiness*. The mind's emptiness is like this: it holds everything and is not any of it. A cup is not improved by removing the water; the point of the cup is the space.

## Thought arising from what?

A passage in this chapter is easy to skim and hard to absorb:

*When true suchness, the self-nature, gives rise to thought, it is not the eyes, ears, nose, tongue that can think. True suchness has a nature, therefore it gives rise to thought; if true suchness were absent, the eyes, ears, forms and sounds would decay on the spot.*

The claim is about the source of a thought. We habitually locate thinking in the sense organs and their objects — a sight triggers a thought, a sound triggers a thought. This says the trigger is not the source. What sees and hears is the six roots; what does not stain the objects is the true nature, *常自在*.

This is also where the chapter saves 无念 from becoming its own caricature. If thought arises from true suchness itself, then no-thought cannot mean no thoughts:

*To know and see all dharmas with a mind unstained — this is no-thought. To use it is to pervade everywhere, yet not to cling anywhere. But to think nothing at all, to cut off thought — this is bondage to dharma, this is a view on the edge.*

That last phrase, *边见*, is the same word used for extreme views. Suppressing thought does not produce equanimity; it produces a fixed position, and a fixed position on the side of blankness is still a position.

## 佛法在世间

The long verse in this chapter ends with the line people quote most:

*The Buddha-dharma is in the world; awakening does not leave the world. Seek bodhi apart from the world and you seek rabbit horns.*

Rabbit horns: an object with no referent. Not a metaphor for something rare — a metaphor for something that cannot be found because it is not the kind of thing that exists.

The verse also contains the diagnostic that keeps this from becoming a slogan about being spiritual at work:

*If you see others' faults, your own fault is the deviation. Others being wrong is not your being wrong; your being wrong is your own fault. Just remove the fault-finding mind and the affliction is broken.*

The world you are told not to leave is not a concept. It is the place where someone else's error irritates you, and the practice is located exactly there.

## The test

Try, for sixty seconds, to stop a thought from finishing. Then notice who was doing the stopping. That second presence — the one with a hand on the valve — is the pairing this chapter dismantles: a watcher and a watched, both manufactured for the exercise. When the sixty seconds end, ask whether anything was actually made quieter, or only covered.
